title: Support, confidence, and interest
summary: Count baskets first, then generate rules from frequent itemsets without confusing support and confidence.
objectives: Compute support from a basket table
Use downward closure to prune candidates

sections.title: Core equations
sections.body: For an itemset $I$, support is the fraction of baskets containing $I$. For a rule $A\to B$, confidence is $\operatorname{supp}(A\cup B)/\operatorname{supp}(A)$. Interest compares confidence with the base rate $\operatorname{supp}(B)$.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Lecture and assignment material define the current study target; the MMDS index is attached as labeled depth, not merged into lecture scope.

sections.title: Visual reading
sections.body: Read the basket table as a set of transactions, not as a graph. The network-like slide decoration is only a visual cue; the formal object is still a basket incidence relation.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which quantity asks how often the entire itemset appears in all baskets?
contrastDrills.explanation: Support uses the full transaction population; confidence conditions on the antecedent.

contrastDrills.prompt: A rule has high confidence because its consequent is common everywhere. Which measure exposes that baseline?
contrastDrills.explanation: Lift compares confidence with the consequent base rate.

contrastDrills.prompt: An itemset is infrequent. What can be pruned safely?
contrastDrills.explanation: Downward closure says every superset has support no larger than the infrequent subset.

math.explanation: Support asks how often every item in $I$ appears together. The numerator counts qualifying baskets; the denominator is the full transaction count. Keep the count and normalized fraction distinct when reporting an answer.
math.name: Itemset support
math.purpose: Use it to measure how often an itemset occurs in the transaction population.

math.explanation: Confidence conditions on baskets that already contain $A$. That is why the denominator is $\operatorname{supp}(A)$ rather than the total number of baskets. A high confidence can still be uninteresting when $B$ is common everywhere.
math.name: Itemset support
math.purpose: Use it to measure how often an itemset occurs in the transaction population.

math.explanation: Lift compares the rule's conditional rate with the base rate of $B$. A value above $1$ means $B$ is more common when $A$ is present than it is overall; it does not prove causation.
math.name: Itemset support
math.purpose: Use it to measure how often an itemset occurs in the transaction population.
math.caveat: Lift is sensitive to rare consequents and should be read with support counts.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Can a rule have high confidence and still be useless? Construct a counterexample.
criticalQuestions.angle: Make $B$ very common and compare the confidence with the base rate of $B$.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Yes. If $B$ appears in almost every basket, then $A\to B$ can have high confidence without $A$ adding much information; lift exposes that issue.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why does downward closure justify pruning, and what does it not justify?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate a guaranteed support property from a heuristic about predictive usefulness.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: If a set is infrequent, every superset is also infrequent, so pruning is safe for frequent-itemset discovery. It says nothing about confidence, lift, or causal value.
